metadata.name: du
metadata.description: Display disk usage of directories and files

installation.note: du is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: du (disk usage) estimates and displays the disk space used by files and directories. Unlike df which shows file system space, du shows how much space specific directories and files are using. Essential for finding what's taking up disk space.

syntax.description: Display disk usage for DIRECTORY/FILE. If no argument, shows usage for current directory and subdirectories.

options.use_case: Show sizes in KB, MB, GB (always use this)

options.description: Show only total for each argument
options.use_case: Show only total size, not subdirectories
Show sizes for current directory and immediate subdirectories only

options.description: Show sizes for all files, not just directories
options.use_case: Show sizes for individual files too

examples.title: Check directory size

output_explanation.notes: Shows total size of directory. -s = summarize (total only), -h = human-readable. Very common pattern.

examples.use_case: Quickly check total size of a directory

examples.title: Find large directories
examples.description: Show sizes of immediate subdirectories, sorted by size

output_explanation.format: Sizes of directories sorted smallest to largest

elements.meaning: Show only current directory and immediate subdirectories

breakdown.useful: Find which subdirectory is using most space
breakdown.common: Very useful pattern for finding large directories

output_explanation.notes: Shows sizes of subdirectories. sort -h sorts by size. Very useful for finding what's taking up space.

examples.use_case: Identify which subdirectories are using the most space

examples.title: Find largest files and directories

elements.meaning: Show all files, not just directories

breakdown.pattern: du -ah shows all, sort -h sorts by size, tail -10 shows largest
breakdown.useful: Find largest files consuming disk space

output_explanation.notes: Shows largest files and directories. Useful for finding what to delete when disk is full.

examples.use_case: Find largest files consuming disk space

examples.title: Check current directory
examples.description: Show total size of current directory

breakdown.simple: Quick check of current directory size
breakdown.useful: Common pattern for checking project size

output_explanation.notes: Shows total size of current directory. Useful for checking project or directory size.

misconceptions.title: du shows file system space
misconceptions.misconception: du displays available file system space
misconceptions.reality: du shows disk USAGE (how much space files/directories use), not available space. Use df to see available file system space.
misconceptions.tip: du = disk usage (how much space is used). df = disk free (how much space is available).

common_pitfalls.description: du output in blocks is hard to read
common_pitfalls.solution: Always use du -h for human-readable format. Much easier to understand sizes.

common_pitfalls.description: du can be slow on very large directory trees
common_pitfalls.solution: Use --max-depth to limit depth, or du specific subdirectories. Be patient on large trees.

related_commands.relationship: File system space; du shows usage, df shows available space
related_commands.description: Show disk space of file systems (complements du)

related_commands.relationship: Find files; du shows sizes, find locates files
related_commands.description: Find files by criteria (can combine with du for large files)

related_commands.relationship: Sort output; often used with du to sort by size
related_commands.description: Sort du output by size (du -h | sort -h)

best_practices: Always use du -h for human-readable output
Use du -sh for total directory size
Use du -h --max-depth=1 to see subdirectory sizes
Combine with sort: du -h | sort -h (sorts by size)
Use du -ah | sort -h | tail to find largest files
Use du to find what's consuming disk space before cleanup
performance_tips: du can be slow on large directory trees
Use --max-depth to limit depth and speed up
du -sh is faster than du -h (summarize only)
Be patient when running on very large directories

additional_notes.human_readable: Always use -h flag for readable output (KB, MB, GB)
additional_notes.vs_df: du = disk usage (how much space files use), df = disk free (available space)
additional_notes.common_patterns: Common: du -sh directory (total), du -h --max-depth=1 (subdirs), du -ah | sort -h | tail (largest)
additional_notes.finding_large_files: Use du -ah | sort -h | tail -10 to find largest files consuming space
